content.text: I'll read the file and review it.

Reviewed. Six real problems across both lenses.

**bugs lens:**
- `os.Open` error discarded (line 10) — a missing file yields a nil `*os.File`, and `f.Read` then returns `ErrInvalid` ("invalid argument") instead of the actual "no such file or directory". The real cause is destroyed.
- File is never closed — fd leak on every call, including the success path.
- Single `f.Read` into a 4096-byte buffer (line 12) — anything past 4096 bytes is silently dropped, and `Read` is permitted to return a short read even on small files. Silent data loss with no error.
- Empty file returns `io.EOF` as an error rather than an empty result.
- `firstName` (line 24) indexes `names[0]` with no length check — panics on an empty slice, which `loadNames` can return.

**impl lens:**
- The godoc says "returns the non-empty names", but the loop appends every trimmed line unconditionally — empty lines and the trailing-newline artifact all end up in the result. The stated filter is simply not implemented.

The whole read path collapses to `os.ReadFile`, which fixes the leak, the truncation and the EOF case at once.

findings.title: Single Read truncates files over 4096 bytes and accepts short reads
findings.body:
`f.Read(buf)` is called once into a fixed 4096-byte buffer. Two failure modes, both silent:

1. Any file larger than 4096 bytes is truncated — the tail is discarded and the function returns success. A names file with 500 entries returns roughly the first 250 with no error.
2. `io.Reader.Read` is explicitly allowed to return fewer bytes than requested even when more are available. A single unlooped `Read` therefore may return a partial file even under 4096 bytes.

On top of that, a truncated read almost always cuts mid-line, so the last returned name is a corrupted fragment rather than a real name. The caller has no way to detect any of this — `err` is nil and the slice looks well-formed.
findings.fix: Replace the manual buffer read with `data, err := os.ReadFile(path)`, which reads to EOF and closes the file. This also removes the fd leak and the empty-file EOF bug in the same change.

findings.title: os.Open error discarded, masking the real failure cause
findings.body:
`f, _ := os.Open(path)` throws away the error. When the open fails, `f` is nil. `(*os.File).Read` guards against a nil receiver via `checkValid`, so this does not panic — it returns `os.ErrInvalid`, and line 14 propagates that to the caller.

The result is that every open failure is reported as `invalid argument`. A missing file, a permission denial, and a path that is actually a directory all collapse into the same useless message, and the original error naming the path is gone. Debugging a bad `path` from the caller side becomes guesswork.
findings.fix: Handle the error at the open site: `f, err := os.Open(path); if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("open %s: %w", path, err) }` — or drop the manual open entirely in favor of `os.ReadFile`.

findings.title: firstName panics on an empty slice
findings.body:
`names[0]` is indexed with no length check, so `firstName(nil)` or `firstName([]string{})` panics with `index out of range [0] with length 0`.

This is directly reachable from the other function in this file: `loadNames` returns `nil, nil` is not possible today, but it does return a slice built from caller-controlled file content, and any future guard added for the empty-file case (see the `io.EOF` finding) produces exactly the empty slice that crashes here. The function also has no godoc stating a non-empty precondition, so a caller has no signal that passing an empty slice is illegal.
findings.fix: Return a zero value for the empty case: `if len(names) == 0 { return "" }` — or change the signature to `(string, bool)` if the caller must distinguish "empty input" from "first name is the empty string".

findings.title: Godoc promises non-empty names but every line is appended unconditionally
findings.body:
The godoc on line 8 states the function "returns the non-empty names in it", but the loop appends `strings.TrimSpace(line)` for every line with no emptiness check. Nothing filters anything.

This is not a hypothetical mismatch — it fires on essentially every real input. A file ending with a trailing newline (the normal case for a text file) makes `strings.Split` produce a final empty element, so the returned slice always carries a trailing `""`. Blank separator lines and whitespace-only lines each contribute another `""`. A caller trusting the documented contract — for example ranging over the result and using each entry as a lookup key or a filename — gets empty strings it was told could not occur.
findings.fix:
Skip empties inside the loop:
```go
name := strings.TrimSpace(line)
if name == "" {
	continue
}
out = append(out, name)
```

findings.title: Opened file is never closed — fd leak on every call
findings.body:
`os.Open` acquires a file descriptor and there is no `defer f.Close()` anywhere in the function. Every code path — the error return on line 14 and the success return on line 20 — leaks the descriptor.

The fd is only reclaimed when the finalizer runs during a GC cycle, which is not a guarantee the code can rely on. In a service that calls `loadNames` repeatedly (a reload loop, a per-request path, a watcher), descriptors accumulate until the process hits `EMFILE`, at which point unrelated opens — sockets, other files — start failing with "too many open files". The failure surfaces far away from this function, which makes it expensive to diagnose.
findings.fix: Add `defer f.Close()` immediately after a successful open, or switch to `os.ReadFile`, which handles closing internally.

findings.title: Empty file returns io.EOF instead of an empty result
findings.body:
For a zero-length file, `f.Read(buf)` returns `n == 0, err == io.EOF`. The check on line 13 treats that as a failure and returns `nil, io.EOF`.

An empty names file is a valid input meaning "no names", not an error condition. The caller must special-case `errors.Is(err, io.EOF)` to distinguish it from a genuine read failure, which is not documented anywhere and is unlikely to be handled. `io.EOF` also leaks an implementation detail of the read strategy into the API — it would disappear the moment the read loop changed.
findings.fix: Covered by switching to `os.ReadFile`, which returns an empty byte slice and a nil error for an empty file. If the manual read is kept, treat EOF as terminal rather than fatal: `if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, io.EOF) { return nil, err }`.
